Stage 7 · Phase prediction and folding

Stage 7a predicts the pulse phase that the receiver should see. Stage 7 folds the data on that phase.

On this page
  1. 7a · Phase prediction: why · makeTrajectory · delayModel · loadEphemeris · makePredictor
  2. 7 · Folding, foldProfile: the phase model · folding a time bin · the weights · correlated time bins · data weights · with a predictor · NBin and sub-int length

7a · Phase prediction for a moving receiver

A pulsar's rotation is a clock at the centre of mass of the solar system, the barycentre. The receiver moves with the Earth and with its ship, so the pulses reach it early or late by up to ±500 s over a year and ±8 ms over a day. This stage predicts that motion, so that the fold (stage 7) stays aligned over hours and days. What the prediction does not explain becomes the position, in stage 10.

Functions: makeTrajectory → delayModel (with loadEphemeris) → makePredictor, run by the observer from the ephemeris and the trajectory it assumes · the fold follows the result: foldProfile('Predictor', …) · the simulator's truth: trueResiduals and the receiver's clock makeClock · frames, time scales and relativity: localisation · block D

7a.1 Why the phase must be predicted

The fold assigns every time bin a pulse phase. Without a predictor it uses a constant spin rate, φ(t) = f₀·(t − TRef), which is only right for a receiver at rest relative to the barycentre. A real receiver moves, so each pulse travels a little longer or shorter. The Earth's orbital speed changes the arrival rate by up to 10⁻⁴, a Doppler shift. Within one 120 s sub-integration that moves the pulse by 12 ms, more than B0329+54's 5 ms core width (Figure 7a.2). For J0437 a 300 s sub-integration drifts by five whole turns. Without a prediction, every fold longer than a few minutes smears out.

This stage therefore computes the delay from the receiver to the barycentre, turns it into a predicted phase, and the fold follows it. In the test, a pulsar with a Doppler factor of 10⁻³ folds as cleanly as one without Doppler: the profiles agree to 10⁻⁸ of the peak.

The delay has several terms:

TermWhat it isSize
Roemer, Earth's orbitLight-travel time across the Earth's offset from the barycentre±412 s per year for B0329+54
Roemer, Earth's rotationThe site turns with the Earth±7.6 ms per day for B0329+54 from 52° N
Roemer, the shipThe receiver's position on the Earth: what navigation wants to find333 µs per 100 km along the line of sight
EinsteinThe receiver's clock runs at a varying rate along the eccentric orbit±1.66 ms per year
ShapiroThe Sun's gravity delays the pulse−17 to +6 µs over a year for B0329+54
Binary orbit (not modelled)J0437 orbits a companion±3.4 s per 5.74 days
Dispersion at the Doppler-shifted frequency (not modelled)The dispersion delay holds at the barycentric frequency, which the Earth's orbit shifts by up to 10⁻⁴±7.1 µs per year for B0329+54

The last two terms are not in delayModel. J0437's binary orbit was parked at the close of block D, because J0437 never rises at 52° N (navigation). The Doppler-shifted dispersion delay cancels in the simulator, so it matters only for real data (limitations). Sections 7a.2–7a.5 build the prediction in three steps: where the receiver is, the delay to the barycentre, and the predicted phase. The fold then follows it (Section 7.6), the fast simulator places the true pulses against it (trueResiduals), and the difference between the two is what navigation measures (stage 10).

History

Block D's design was agreed on 21 Oct 2026: an analytic Earth orbit first and DE440 at the end, and a phase predictor with a trajectory interface, for sensor fusion. Later the same day it was decided that the observer folds with its own clock estimate. Steps D1 (where the receiver is, the delays) and D2 (the predictor, the fold that follows it) were built on 21 Oct. Their tests pass in Jasper's run of 22 Oct.

7a.2 makeTrajectory: where the receiver is validated

traj = makeTrajectory(type, ...)

Full interface and help text of makeTrajectory →

makeTrajectory describes where the receiver is at any time: one struct with a position function and a velocity function. The delay model and the predictor only ever see this struct, so they work the same for every kind of receiver. The end goal is sensor fusion, in which a motion predictor such as a Kalman filter supplies the trajectory; the 'custom' type is where it plugs in, and nothing else in block D needs to know what kind of vehicle it is.

TypeThe receiverFrame
'fixed'A site on the ground, given as latitude, longitude and height. An offset in east, north and up can move it, for example to put the true site 100 km from the assumed one.Earth-fixed
'track'A ship, given as waypoints in time. The positions between them are interpolated: linearly, smoothly (pchip) or as a cubic spline.Earth-fixed
'barycentric'A deep-space probe, given as positions relative to the barycentre.Barycentric
'custom'Anything that can return positions, such as a Kalman filter's propagated state.Either

Times are seconds since J2000.0 (1 January 2000, 12:00 TT). Positions are in metres. The Earth-fixed frame rotates with the Earth; the delay model adds that rotation.

Options and outputs
Options
Lat, Lon, Height (0 m), OffsetENU ([0 0 0] m) for 'fixed'; Time with Lat, Lon, Height for 'track', or with Pos for 'barycentric', and Interp ('linear'; or 'pchip', 'spline') for both; Frame ('ECEF'), PosFcn, VelFcn, VelStep (1 s: the step of the numerical velocity when no VelFcn is given) for 'custom'
Output
type, frame, pos and vel (functions of time, m and m/s), tRange (where it is valid), params; for 'fixed' also ecef (the point) and enu (its local east, north and up unit vectors)

Tests (tests/testMakeTrajectory.m). The positions and velocities agree with closed forms and with an independent conversion back to latitude and longitude.

TestWhat it checksResult
1 · Fixed siteThe ellipsoid geometry, and an offset of 100 km east.Back to latitude and longitude to 10⁻¹⁰°. The offset is 100.000000 km, exactly horizontal.
2–3 · Ship trackWaypoints, legs, and the velocity.Waypoints exact. The smooth track's velocity equals its derivative to 2·10⁻⁸ m/s and is continuous at turns.
4 · Across 180° longitudeA track crossing the date line.The midpoint lies on 180.00000000°.
5 · Probe orbitA 1 AU orbit sampled hourly, as a spline.Within 1 mm of the true circle.
6–7 · Custom, inputsThe filter entry point; bad inputs.The default velocity is exact for uniform motion. Four bad inputs are refused.
History

Added 21 Oct 2026 as step D1a. The 'spline' option was added while writing the test: pchip leaves metres of error on an hourly orbit, the spline 1 mm.

7a.3 delayModel: from the receiver to the barycentre validated

d = delayModel(t, traj, psr, ...)

Full interface and help text of delayModel →

delayModel gives the time to add to the receiver's arrival time to get the arrival time at the barycentre: the total and each term separately. It works in three steps.

  1. The Earth: by default, the centre of mass of the Earth and Moon follows a Keplerian orbit around the Sun, from JPL's approximate orbital elements. Jupiter and Saturn move the Sun around the barycentre, by about 0.005 AU, and the Moon moves the Earth around the Earth–Moon centre by about 4700 km. With 'Ephemeris' the Earth and the Sun come from JPL's DE440 instead (Section 7a.4).
  2. The receiver: an Earth-fixed position is turned with the Earth's rotation angle and added to the Earth's position. With 'Ephemeris' it is turned with the Earth's real axis instead: precession, nutation and apparent sidereal time. A barycentric trajectory is used as it is.
  3. The terms: the Roemer delay projects the receiver's position onto the direction of the pulsar. The Einstein and Shapiro delays are added from their standard formulas.
The formulas and their signs

With r the receiver relative to the barycentre and n̂ the unit vector to the pulsar:

\[ \Delta = t_\mathrm{SSB} - t = \frac{\mathbf r\cdot\hat n}{c} \;-\; \frac{|\mathbf r|^2 - (\mathbf r\cdot\hat n)^2}{2cD} \;+\; \Delta_E \;+\; 2T_\odot \ln\frac{|\mathbf r_\odot| + \mathbf r_\odot\cdot\hat n}{\mathrm{AU}} \]
  • The first term is the Roemer delay. A receiver displaced towards the pulsar gets each pulse earlier, so the barycentre's time is later.
  • The second term corrects for the curved wave front of a pulsar at distance D. It is about 1 µs for B0329+54.
  • ΔE = TDB − TT is the Einstein delay: 1.657 ms·sin g + 14 µs·sin 2g, with g the Earth's mean anomaly, plus a site term vE·rsite/c² of about 1 µs. With 'Ephemeris' the first two terms are replaced by TDB − TT integrated from DE440 (loadEphemeris).
  • The last term is minus the Shapiro delay. Here r⊙ is the receiver relative to the Sun, and T⊙ = GM⊙/c³ = 4.925 µs. It becomes strongly negative when the Sun is close to the line of sight.

An analytic Earth for simulations, DE440 for real data. The analytic orbit puts the Earth within about 1.5·10⁴ km of its true distance from the Sun, but the Sun itself is off by up to 3·10⁵ km from the barycentre, because the model leaves out Uranus and Neptune. B0329+54's Roemer delay is then off by up to 0.66 s, and 71 ms of that varies within two years. In the simulator this does not matter: the true and the predicted delays come from the same model, and only their difference reaches the navigation fit, which is the same with either orbit to 2·10⁻¹² s. Real data need DE440, accurate to centimetres, plus precession and nutation of the Earth's axis. delayModel takes it behind the same interface, with the option 'Ephemeris'. The analytic orbit stays the default, so every simulation keeps its numbers.

What delayModel leaves out
  • Dispersion. The predictor takes the dispersion delay at the reference frequency as a constant, part of the phase reference. Against real data that misses the annual term of the Doppler-shifted dispersion delay: ±7.1 µs for B0329+54, ±0.3 µs for J0437 (limitations).
  • UT1 − UTC and polar motion. 'DeltaT' (TT − UT1) is one number, 69.184 s by default; the real value changes by up to about 0.9 s, which moves a site by up to about 0.4 km (260 m at 52° N; localisation). Polar motion is about 10 m.
  • A binary orbit (Section 7a.1).
Options and outputs
Options
Terms (all four: "roemer", "curvature", "einstein", "shapiro"), Moon (true), Planets (true: Jupiter and Saturn move the Sun), Ephemeris (none: the analytic orbit; or a loadEphemeris struct; Moon and Planets then do not apply), DeltaT (69.184 s: TT − UT1, for the Earth's rotation)
Output
total and each term (roemer, curvature, einstein, shapiro) in seconds; rObs, vObs (the receiver relative to the barycentre); rEarth, vEarth, rSun; nHat (the direction to the pulsar); frame; model

Tests (tests/testDelayModel.m). Each term agrees with a closed form computed independently in the test.

TestWhat it checksResult

History

Added 21 Oct 2026 as step D1b. Three corrections were made to the test while writing it, none to the model. The annual closed form needs the eccentricity at the date of each extreme. The extremes had to be found on a grid finer than one hour. The amplitude tolerance had to allow for the one-minute grid. The 'Ephemeris' option and test 10 were added on 22 Oct 2026 (step D5b). The comparison with DE440 showed that the analytic orbit's absolute error had been understated: 10⁴ km holds for the Earth relative to the Sun, not for the barycentre. Precession, nutation and the 'DeltaT' option followed the same day with test 11 (step D5d). Test 10's bound on the 100 km measurement then had to allow for the turn of the real axis.

7a.4 loadEphemeris: JPL's DE440 validated

eph = loadEphemeris(file); [r, v] = eph.earth(t)

Full interface and help text of loadEphemeris →

JPL's planetary ephemeris DE440 gives the positions of the Sun, the Earth and the Moon relative to the barycentre; for the Earth today it is accurate to well below a metre. loadEphemeris reads JPL's binary file once and returns functions that evaluate it, in the same way as a trajectory.

  1. The file: de440s.bsp from JPL's NAIF server, 32.7 MB, covering 1850 to 2150, in data/ephem/.
  2. The segments: each body has a sequence of equal time intervals, each holding Chebyshev polynomial coefficients for x, y and z.
  3. Evaluation: the time selects the interval; the polynomials give the position, and their derivatives the velocity.
  4. The chain: the file stores the Earth relative to the Earth–Moon barycentre, and that barycentre relative to the solar-system barycentre. The function adds the links up.
  5. TDB − TT: at loading, the function integrates the rate of a clock at the geocentre along the Earth's path, every 6 hours over the whole file, from the Earth's speed and the potential of the Sun, the Moon and the planets. The integral takes 0.8 s and replaces the analytic model's two terms.

The time is TDB, the ephemeris' own time scale. The frame is ICRF, which is the J2000 equator and equinox to 0.02″. The function reads JPL's file directly, rather than through MATLAB's planetEphemeris from the Aerospace Toolbox (not installed) or JPL's SPICE toolkit (a large external dependency): the format is simple, and about 60 lines of MATLAB read it. JPL's own Horizons service then checks the result to centimetres.

Tests (tests/testLoadEphemeris.m). The Earth from the file agrees with JPL's Horizons service to a few centimetres.

TestWhat it checksResult
1 · HorizonsThe geocentre relative to the barycentre at three dates between 2000 and 2045, against JPL's Horizons service (DE441).Within 4.5 cm and 1.1·10⁻⁷ m/s.
2 · VelocityThe velocity against a central difference of the position.Within 1.1·10⁻⁶ m/s.
3 · Earth and MoonThe two balance about their barycentre with the Earth/Moon mass ratio.81.300568, the same at every time to 10⁻¹².
4 · TDB − TTThe integral against the USNO series (USNO Circular 179), stated good to about 10 µs, from 2000 to 2050.2.25 µs rms, 7.1 µs at most. The analytic two terms are 16.5 µs rms and 33 µs at most off the same series.
5 · InputsA missing file, a file that is not SPK, an unknown body, a time outside the file.Refused.
History

Added 22 Oct 2026 as step D5a, the first step of block D's last part. The file was downloaded from NAIF the same day, after Jasper's go-ahead for D5. TDB − TT followed the same day (step D5c). A first comparison removed a linear trend from the integral; that trend is real over 2000–2050, and the published series has it too.

7a.5 makePredictor: the predicted pulse phase validated

pred = makePredictor(psr, traj, [t1 t2], ...)

Full interface and help text of makePredictor →

makePredictor computes the pulse phase the receiver should see, once per observation, and stores it as short polynomials, so that the fold only has to evaluate them.

  1. The phase at the barycentre: φ = Φ₀ + f₀·(tSSB − TRef) + ½·F1·(tSSB − TRef)², the pulsar's timing model.
  2. The arrival time: a pulse received at time t reaches the barycentre at tSSB = t + Δ(t), with Δ from delayModel.
  3. Segments: the span is cut into one-hour segments. In each, the phase is fitted with a Chebyshev polynomial of degree 12.
  4. Checks: each segment is compared with the direct computation between its fitting points. A segment that misses 1 ns is split in two, until it passes. A ship's sharp turn is the typical case: around it the segments shrink to a few seconds (Figure 7a.3).

The predictor returns the phase and the observed spin frequency, which includes the Doppler shift. The receiver's samples are timed by its own oscillator, so the data's time stamps are clock readings, not true time. With the option 'Clock' the predictor gets the observer's estimate of its clock error, and turns each clock reading into its best estimate of true time before it computes the delays. A commercial SDR's oscillator is specified to ±2 ppm; without this correction that rate would move the pulse by 240 µs within a 120 s sub-integration, like an uncorrected Doppler shift.

Radio observatories work the same way: they compute "polycos" before an observation. It keeps all the physics out of the streaming fold, which only evaluates a polynomial, and that is also the interface an FPGA or GPU version needs. The trajectory is the predictor's only input about the receiver, so a motion predictor plugs in without touching the fold.

Precision

Absolute times (about 8·10⁸ s) and absolute phases (up to about 10¹¹ turns) lose precision in double arithmetic. So the polynomials hold the phase counted from the integer turn at the start of the span, as a function of the time since that start. Only one constant carries the rounding of the large numbers, about 10⁻⁶ turns, and it is the same for every segment. There are therefore no steps between segments.

Options and outputs
Options
SegLength (3600 s), Degree (12), Tol (10⁻⁹ s: the check every segment must pass), MinSeg (1 s: the shortest segment), DelayArgs (options passed on to delayModel, such as 'Ephemeris'), Clock (none; the observer's clock estimate)
Output
phase and freq (functions of the time since the span's start: the phase in turns since the integer turn N0, and the observed spin frequency), tOrigin, N0, frac0, seg and coef (the segments and their Chebyshev coefficients), fRange, maxErr (the largest timing error the checks found), clock, tOriginTrue. Outside its span it refuses with makePredictor:range.

Tests (tests/testMakePredictor.m). The predicted phase agrees with the timing model evaluated directly, to well within 1 ns.

The predictor is now ready. Stage 7 folds the detected power on it.

7 · Folding: foldProfile validated

[info, fold] = foldProfile(info_det, outFile, f0, 'F1', F1, 'TRef', TRef, 'NBin', nBin, 'SubintPeriods', n, ...)

Full interface and help text of foldProfile → · used by both front ends; the channel path adds 'NoiseCoeffs' (no excision) or 'DataWeights' (with excision)

Folding averages all turns at the same rotational phase, so the pulse adds up and the noise averages down. The fold keeps not just the profile, but everything needed to know its noise exactly: how much data went into every phase bin, and how strongly neighbouring bins share noise.

7.1 The phase model

For a receiver at rest the phase comes from the ephemeris alone, observer knowledge only:

(7.1)\[ \phi(t) = \Phi_0 + f_0\,(t - T_\mathrm{ref}) + \tfrac{1}{2}\,F_1\,(t - T_\mathrm{ref})^2 \]
\(\phi(t)\)
rotational phase at time \(t\) [turns]
\(t\)
time of a detected time bin [s]
\(T_\mathrm{ref}\)
reference epoch [s] ('TRef' option, from ephem.TRef)
\(\Phi_0\)
phase at \(T_\mathrm{ref}\) [turns] ('Phi0', default 0)
\(f_0\)
spin frequency at \(T_\mathrm{ref}\) [Hz] (f0 input, ephem.f0)
\(F_1\)
its time derivative [Hz/s] ('F1', ephem.F1 = 0)

Tref is the first true pulse centre (T/2, from ephem.TRef), and Φ0 = 0, so every true pulse peak is at a whole number of turns. A moving receiver uses the predicted phase of Section 7a.5 instead (Section 7.6). Each detected time bin is assigned to phase bins by its phase, and averaging over N turns improves the SNR by √N (Figure 7.1).

The fold works on detected power, after dedispersion. The pulsar is noise whose power changes with phase, so the profile is a profile of power: square first, then fold, then match the template (full-band page). After dedispersion, each time bin already holds every frequency of the same instant. The turns are cut halfway between pulses: with ephem.TRef at a pulse centre, the cut at φ = k + ½ falls in the off-pulse region, so a pulse is never split between two sub-ints. The pulse sits at phase 0, the start of the stored profile (and wraps to its end), which is where the TOA fit expects the template.

7.2 Folding a time bin

  1. Skip it unless it saw the complete dedispersion sweep (fullySupportedBins).
  2. Phase: compute its rotational phase φ, in double precision.
  3. Turn and place: the nearest whole number of φ is its turn; the rest, between −½ and ½, is its place in the profile.
  4. Share it between the two nearest phase bins (linear assignment, Figure 7.2), and add it to that sub-int's sums.
  5. Divide: the profile of each sub-int is its sum divided by how much data went in. Alongside, the fold keeps what is needed to know the noise of every phase bin exactly (Section 7.3).
The exact rules
  1. Use only fullySupportedBins (data that saw the complete dedispersion sweep).
  2. Phase per time bin, in double.
  3. turn = round(φ), frac = φ − turn ∈ [−½, ½]: each turn runs from half a turn before its pulse to half a turn after, so cuts fall between pulses.
  4. NBin phase bins; bin j (1-based) is centred at phase (j−1)/NBin; negative phases wrap to the end. Position x = frac·NBin.
  5. Linear assignment (default): j0 = ⌊x⌋, a = x − j0; the time bin contributes with weight 1 − a to bin j0 and a to bin j0 + 1.
  6. Accumulate per (phase bin, sub-int, channel): sum Σw·P, weight Σw, weight2, weightX (below).
  7. Sub-integrations of SubintPeriods turns (or SubintTime); prof = sum/weight; profTotal = Σsum/Σweight over all sub-ints.
  8. Per sub-int: turnRef (the middle turn), tRef = the time where φ = turnRef (stable quadratic root), fRef = spin frequency at tRef, tMean, nTimeBins. These define the TOA later.
  9. Saved to a .mat file (fold + info). Vectorized accumarray, chunked reading.

Linear assignment preserves each sample's mean position exactly. Nearest-bin assignment ('nearest') gave a 0.5 ns bias: the 1 µs time grid and the 9.765625 µs phase grid repeat identically every turn, so the rounding errors do not average out (Figure 7.3). The price is that neighbouring phase bins share data, so their noise is correlated, which the fold tracks explicitly.

7.3 The weights

For phase bin j of one sub-int, sumj = Σk akj·Pk, with akj how much of time bin k went into phase bin j. Three fields describe how the data were combined:

FieldFormulaPurpose
weightΣk akj (with data weights: Σ a·W)normalizer: how much data is in bin j; prof = sum/weight
weight2Σk akj² (× V, plus lag terms)var(profj) = σ²·weight2/weight² (variance of a weighted mean)
weightX(:,:,:,d)Σ akj·ak,j+d (× correlations)cov(profj, profj+d) = σ²·weightX/(weightj·weightj+d)

An example. A time bin 30 % of the way from bin j to j+1 is split 0.7 and 0.3. It adds 0.49 and 0.09 to the two weight2 values, and 0.21 to weightX. Over many turns the ratios settle at W : W2 : WX = 1 : 2/3 : 1/6: a neighbour correlation of 0.25, exactly the 0.2484 measured in the long noise-only run.

weightX matters; it was a real bug once. With linear assignment, a phase bin's variance per turn looks like (2/3)·σ²/n instead of σ²/n, with n the number of time bins per phase bin:

Phase binsApparent varianceIndependent-bin value
1024 (where the bug was found)σ²/14.7σ²/9.77
2048 with 0.96 µs channel bins (today)σ²/7.6σ²/5.09

Ignoring the positive covariance between neighbours therefore underestimates the variance of any sum over bins, such as a TOA or a matched filter, by about 1.5×. Until weightX was added, the fold check predicted a centroid scatter of 0.226 µs instead of the correct 0.277 µs (bugs and lessons #8).

σ² itself is not stored in the fold. The consumers (estimateTOA, detectPulsar) compute it from their own noise model: the radiometer equation with the fitted level, or the off-pulse residuals. The fold only stores how the data were combined, so one fold serves both noise models, and the fold never needs the true noise level, which only the simulator knows.

7.4 Correlated time bins: 'NoiseCoeffs'

In a narrow channel, neighbouring detected time bins are correlated. Relative to σ² = m²/(B·Δt), a bin has variance V, and covariance X(L) with the bin L places further (powerCovariance). The covariance of two phase-bin sums is then

(7.2)\[ \operatorname{cov}(S_j, S_{j+d}) = \sigma^2 \sum_k \sum_{k'} a_{kj}\, a_{k',\,j+d}\; c(k' - k), \qquad c(0) = V, \quad c(\pm L) = X(L) \]
\(S_j\)
the sum in phase bin \(j\) of one sub-int: \(\sum_k a_{kj}\,\times\) power of time bin \(k\) (fold.sum)
\(j\), \(d\)
phase-bin index; phase-bin lag (1 … \(D\))
\(k, k'\)
time-bin indices
\(a_{kj}\)
assignment weight of time bin \(k\) to phase bin \(j\) (linear assignment: split between the two nearest phase bins)
\(\sigma^2\)
variance of one independent time bin, \(m^2/(B\,\Delta t)\) (radiometer value; not stored in the fold)
\(c(L)\)
correlation coefficient of time bins \(L\) apart, relative to \(\sigma^2\)
\(V\), \(X(L)\)
from powerCovariance ('NoiseCoeffs'); 0 beyond Lmax
  • 'NoiseCoeffs' = [V X(1..Lmax)]; default 1 = independent bins (full band), bit-identical to before.
  • weight2 = var(Sj)/σ², weightX = cov(Sj, Sj+d)/σ² for phase lags d = 1..D, with D = ⌈Lmax·binDt·f·NBin⌉ + 1 (3 for the channel data at 10 ms / 2048 bins).
  • Every pair of time bins L apart in the same sub-int adds X(L)·a·a′ to its pair of phase bins; the last Lmax time bins of a chunk are kept for pairs with the next chunk (addLagPairs).
  • Effect for the channel data: the phase-bin variance is 0.987 of the old model, and the lag-1 correlation 0.258 instead of 0.250.

Tests (tests/testFoldWeights.m 1–3). The four reference folds from before this option reproduce bit for bit, and weight2 and weightX equal Aᵀ·C·A, built explicitly, to 6·10⁻¹⁶. The measured fold noise on 128-channel data fits the new model and clearly rejects the old one:

Measured − predictedNew modelOld model (independent bins)
Variance−1.4σ−13.1σ
Lag-1 covariance+0.6σ+5.9σ

7.5 Data weights per channel: 'DataWeights'

With excision, every detected bin k of channel c has its own numbers, all exact from blankingWeights: a mean Wkc·mc (with W the valid fraction), a variance Vkc·σc², and a covariance Xkc(L)·σc² with bin k+L. The fold uses them:

  • weight = Σ a·W, so prof = Σa·P / Σa·W is unbiased even when blanking depends on pulse phase;
  • weight2 and weightX as in Section 7.4, with the per-bin Vk and Xk(L);
  • a time bin with W = 0 adds no power to the sum either; leftovers from filter tails in such bins biased nearly empty phase bins (found while building blankingWeights);
  • output arrays get a channel dimension: weight, weight2 [NBin × nSub × nChan], weightX [NBin × nSub × nChan × D]; prof, profTotal per channel with its own weights;
  • option value: an info struct with file, nChan, N, Lmax, byteOrder; replaces NoiseCoeffs (error if both).

Dividing by Σa·W rather than Σa makes a bin with W = 0.5 count as half a sample, with the right mean: it contributes half the power to the numerator and 0.5 to the denominator. A fully blanked bin contributes nothing. A test with fake blanking at phase 0.30–0.36 shows the difference: the weighted fold is unbiased (−0.0019 ± 0.0009), while a naive fold is off by −0.574, exactly the predicted 1 − 0.425.

Tests (tests/testFoldWeights.m 4–6). A weight file of constants gives the NoiseCoeffs fold bit for bit. Random weight streams give AᵀW and AᵀCA to 7·10⁻¹⁶. The fake-blanking fold is unbiased, with the noise as modelled. Cost: 1.8 s for 0.1 s of 128 channels with weights, 0.25 s without.

History

'NoiseCoeffs': step A1a, 7 Oct 2026. 'DataWeights': step A1b, the same day. The rule for bins with W = 0 was found in step A3a (blankingWeights).

7.6 Folding with a predictor: 'Predictor' validated

foldProfile takes the predictor of Section 7a.5 with the option 'Predictor'. Each time bin then gets its phase from the predictor instead of Eq. (7.1). The predictor must be built with its start at the recording's time zero. Each sub-integration still gets a reference time and frequency, so that a TOA is the reference time plus the fitted phase offset divided by the frequency. The reference time is where the predicted phase reaches the sub-integration's middle turn. For a partial last sub-integration that turn can fall just after the data; there the phase continues linearly with the last frequency. Without a predictor nothing changes: the constant-rate fold is bit for bit the same.

The tests fold synthetic power series with a known phase. The voltage generator has a fixed period, so the voltage chain has never folded with a predictor. The fast simulator draws its folds in the predictor's frame, and shifts each sub-int's pulse by what the predictor misses (fast simulator).

Tests (tests/testFoldPredictor.m). Folding with a predictor removes the Doppler shift completely.

2 · Without itThe same data folded at a constant rate.Smeared: the peak is 2 % of the true one.
3 · ReferencesEach sub-integration's reference time and frequency.Exact to 6·10⁻¹⁴ turns, also for the partial last one.
4 · No delaysA predictor without delays against the old fold.Identical to 5·10⁻¹¹.
5 · InputsA predictor that is too short, or not a predictor.Refused.
6 · MergingmergeSubints on the predictor fold: 100-turn sub-ints merged in pairs, against the fold with 200 turns per sub-int. A group whose reference turn falls in a gap.Sums and weights equal to 10⁻¹². Reference times equal to 10⁻¹¹ s; the f0 model would be off by 17 ms. The gap is refused.
History

Added 21 Oct 2026 as step D2b. The first version clamped the reference time to the predictor's span, which left the partial last sub-integration 0.39 turns off. It now extrapolates linearly.

Test 6 added 23 Oct 2026 (review of blocks C and D, item A-1). Before it, mergeSubints took the merged reference time from the f0 model for every fold. For a predictor fold that is off by about the Doppler factor times the time since the file's start: 0.3 s per hour of recording for B0329+54.

7.7 Choosing NBin and the sub-int length

NBin = 2048 is more than enough. Binning only costs information if bins are coarse compared with the pulse: σeff² ≈ σt² + Δ²/12. For the simulated pulsar Δ²/12 ÷ σt² = 4·10⁻⁵, for J0437 2·10⁻⁴: negligible. A rule of thumb is NBin ≳ 10·P/W50 (~400 for J0437). Detection and matched-filter SNR do not depend on NBin once bins are fine. What NBin does change is cost: the weights scale as NBin × sub-ints × channels × lags, so long observations will likely use fewer bins or sub-bands.

NBin and f_out together: every phase bin needs data

Consecutive time bins are f·binDt·NBin phase bins apart. If that is above 1, a sub-int can leave phase bins empty, and estimateTOA and detectPulsar (MinCoverage 1) then reject every sub-int. In the f_out sweep, f_out = 100 kHz (10.08 µs bins) with NBin 2048 and 1 turn per sub-int filled only 1984 of the 2048 bins, and that run gave no TOAs at all. foldProfile therefore checks the time grid of the first complete sub-int before folding. If bins would stay empty, it warns (foldProfile:coverage) and names the fixes: NBin ≤ time bins per turn, binDt ≤ 1/(f·NBin), or more turns per sub-int. Main's settings, 0.96 µs time bins and 4.9 µs phase bins, are far inside the limit.

History

The check exists since 9 Oct 2026, after the f_out sweep.

Why sub-integrations. One profile of all turns gives the same precision as the weighted mean of per-sub-int TOAs (for a constant profile and an exact phase model). Sub-ints are there to validate the error bars, to see drift (phase-model errors, motion, clock, position error: the navigation signal itself) and to catch bad data (notes §12).

Sub-int length: SNR ≥ 6–7. Below an SNR of about 6 per sub-int, TOAs start to lock onto noise peaks (threshold sweep). The number of turns per sub-int is therefore N = (SNRtarget/SNRturn)² (Figure 7.4). Here SNRturn ≈ 373·ρ, the flat-band value; with the real band tapers it is 368·ρ on the full band and 360·ρ on the channel path, which needs about 3 % and 7 % more turns. For long observations the length can also be chosen from the data. adaptiveSubints folds into short sub-ints, and merges consecutive ones until the merged profile reaches SNR ~7. This matters when scintillation changes the flux from hour to hour (fast simulator).

Limits

Not stored: covariance between consecutive sub-ints

With correlated time bins, the last bins of one sub-int correlate with the first of the next. Only the 2–3 phase bins at the boundary (phase 0.5, off-pulse) are affected, by ~1–4 % of their variance. Negligible for TOAs (template slope ≈ 0 there) and detection (~10⁻⁵).

Summary
  • A moving receiver sees the pulses Doppler-shifted, by up to 10⁻⁴ from the Earth's orbit alone, so the fold needs a predicted phase.
  • Stage 7a builds it from a trajectory, the delays to the barycentre (Roemer, Einstein, Shapiro) and the timing model, stored as Chebyshev segments that are checked to 1 ns.
  • Stage 7 folds every fully supported time bin by linear assignment, and keeps weight, weight2 and weightX, so that the noise of every phase bin is known exactly (Eq. 7.2), with or without blanking.
  • Sub-ints are long enough for an SNR of 6–7, and NBin = 2048 is fine enough to lose nothing.

Each sub-int's profile now goes to the TOA fit of stage 8 (TOA estimation). The next page in reading order, the fast simulator, draws such folds directly for runs of days.
